extracted.intended_audience: advanced high-school or undergraduate mathematics students (readers of a mathematics textbook)
extracted.subtask_short: studying number systems and complex numbers
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and worked-theory on cardinality and foundations of sets, the introduction and algebra/geometry of complex numbers, roots of unity, the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, and algebraic vs transcendental numbers. Suitable as a textbook chapter for learners developing rigorous understanding and problem-solving skills in these topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of sets and cardinal number
rubrics_metrics.description: If two sets A and B (finite or infinite) are equivalent (there exists a one-to-one correspondence) we say they have the same cardinal number. This generalizes the ordinary notion of the same natural number for finite sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that finite sets with different sizes cannot be equivalent, but infinite sets can be equivalent even if one is a proper subset (e.g., integers vs even integers, rationals vs integers). Uses examples to distinguish denumerable (countable) infinity and the continuum (non-denumerable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor’s theorem (power set has greater cardinality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any set A, the set B of all subsets of A (the power set) has a strictly greater cardinal number than A; i.e., there is no bijection between A and its power set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketches Cantor's diagonal-like argument: assume a bijection correlates each a∈A to a subset S_a⊆A, construct T = {x∈A : x∉S_x} and show T cannot be S_a for any a, yielding contradiction. Notes this produces an infinite hierarchy of increasingly larger infinities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between constructive and non-constructive (indirect) proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a difference between proving existence by providing a concrete example (constructive proof) and proving existence by showing non-existence leads to contradiction (non-constructive/indirect proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains philosophical and practical implications: constructive proofs yield tangible objects, while indirect proofs only produce a contradiction; mentions intuitionism advocating constructive methods and the practical difficulties of banning non-constructive proofs; historical/contextual commentary about resistance to pure intuitionism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Russell’s paradox and necessity for foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: Unrestricted set comprehension leads to contradictions such as Russell's paradox: the set C of all 'ordinary' sets (those not containing themselves) both must and must not contain itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates the paradox by defining ordinary vs extraordinary sets and constructing C, showing the contradiction that arises whether C contains itself or not. Uses this as motivation for more careful foundational systems (restrictions/postulates) in set theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational positions: formalism vs intuitionism
rubrics_metrics.description: Different schools interpret mathematical existence differently: formalists (Hilbert) view existence as 'freedom from contradiction' and aim to formalize mathematics from axioms; intuitionists demand constructive existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes Gödel's results which limit Hilbert's program and emphasizes that even in formalist programs, constructive intuition remains important in mathematics. Provides historical context and implications for the foundations of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a complex number
rubrics_metrics.description: A complex number is defined as a symbol of the form a + bi where a and b are real numbers and i is the imaginary unit with i^2 = -1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduces real part a and imaginary part b; motivates extension of number systems to solve quadratic equations like x^2 = -1; treats i as a symbol subject to the rule i^2 = -1 and accepts complex symbols if they preserve algebraic rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic rules for addition and multiplication of complex numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Addition and multiplication of complex numbers are defined by treating i algebraically and replacing i^2 by -1: (a+bi)+(c+di) = (a+c) + (b+d)i; (a+bi)(c+di) = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives explicit formulas and examples; derives formula for product of conjugates (a+bi)(a-bi) = a^2 + b^2; emphasizes closure under subtraction and division (division formula shown), with exclusion of division by zero when c+di=0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex numbers form a field (contain reals and pure imaginaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of complex numbers is a field: closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication and (nonzero) division. Real numbers embed as a+0i; pure imaginary numbers are 0+bi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes verification of commutative, associative, distributive laws; points out division formula and the special case excluding division by zero; gives examples of arithmetic in complex numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric (Argand) interpretation of complex numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent z = x + yi by the point (x,y) in the plane (number plane); the real part is the x-coordinate, imaginary part is y-coordinate; conjugation reflects in the x-axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines modulus |z| = sqrt(x^2 + y^2) as distance from origin; shows |z|=0 iff z=0; notes multiplicativity of modulus |z1 z2| = |z1||z2| and locates numbers of modulus 1 on the unit circle. Exercises ask to prove these properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallelogram law for addition and triangle inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum z1+z2 corresponds to the fourth vertex of the parallelogram determined by 0, z1, z2; hence |z1+z2| ≤ |z1| + |z2| (triangle inequality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides geometric justification via vector addition and triangle side-length inequality; includes exercise asking when equality holds. Useful for reasoning about magnitudes and distances in the plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polar/trigonometric (modulus–argument) representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Any nonzero complex number z can be written z = p(cos θ + i sin θ), where p = |z| is the modulus and θ is an argument (angle), determined up to integer multiples of 360°.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives relations x = p cos θ, y = p sin θ; notes non-uniqueness of argument (θ + k·360°). Demonstrates conversion examples and sets up trig form for multiplication and exponentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication as rotation and scaling
rubrics_metrics.description: In polar form, multiplication multiplies moduli and adds arguments: if z = p(cos θ + i sin θ) and z' = p'(cos θ' + i sin θ'), then zz' = pp'(cos(θ+θ') + i sin(θ+θ')).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: multiplying by a unit-modulus complex rotates a vector by the specified angle; if modulus ≠1, the length also scales. Includes diagrams/figures and examples (e.g., multiply by i rotates by 90°).

rubrics_metrics.name: De Moivre’s formula
rubrics_metrics.description: For any integer n, (cos θ + i sin θ)^n = cos(nθ) + i sin(nθ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derives from repeated multiplication in polar form; uses to obtain identities for cos(nθ) and sin(nθ) expressed in powers of cosθ and sinθ (examples shown for n=3), and sets up exercises for further derivations and applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: nth roots of unity and the cyclotomic equation
rubrics_metrics.description: The n distinct nth roots of 1 in the complex plane are the vertices of the regular n-gon inscribed in the unit circle; they are 1, α, α^2, …, α^{n-1} where α = cos(360°/n) + i sin(360°/n). They satisfy x^n - 1 = 0 and (except 1) the cyclotomic equation x^{n-1} + x^{n-2} + … + x + 1 = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains geometric construction and algebraic reduction via factorization x^n - 1 = (x-1)(x^{n-1}+…+1). Gives examples (cube roots, fifth roots), reduction tricks (introducing w = x + 1/x) to reduce degrees and construct polygons, and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
rubrics_metrics.description: Every nonconstant polynomial f(x) of degree n with real or complex coefficients has at least one complex root; hence it can be factored into exactly n linear factors over the complex numbers (counting multiplicity): f(x) = ∏_{k=1}^n (x - a_k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch of proof strategy uses Gauss's theorem to find a root, then factor out (x - a) and iterate (induction) to obtain full factorization. Examples include factoring x^4 - 1 into linear factors over C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of algebraic and transcendental numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: An algebraic number is a real or complex number that satisfies some polynomial equation with integer coefficients (degree ≥1). A transcendental number is a real number that is not algebraic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that rational numbers are algebraic (degree 1), irrational algebraic numbers have degree >1. Uses Cantor's theorem to show algebraic numbers are countable, hence transcendental numbers exist. Notes that proving specific numbers transcendental (e.g., e, π) is nontrivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liouville’s theorem on Diophantine approximation and construction of transcendental numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: If z is an algebraic number of degree n > 1, then it cannot be approximated 'too closely' by rational numbers: there exists a bound so that |z - p/q| < 1/q^{n+1} can hold only finitely often (inequality form given).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses this limitation to construct explicit transcendental numbers (Liouville numbers) by producing real numbers with decimal expansions that admit exceptionally good rational approximations (e.g., sums with denominators m!); provides the outline of Liouville's construction and its relation to Cantor's nonconstructive existence proof.
